cards.name: the Wave Code letters
cards.pat: \bwhat (does|do|is) (the |my )?(letter )?(q|s|f|t|d|n|e|a)( (mean|means|stand|stands|in|for|letter)\b|$)|\b(letters?|quick spark|slow simmer|nuanced|explicit|attuned)\b[^?]*\b(wave ?codes?|wavelength)\b|\b(wave ?codes?|wavelength)\b[^?]*\b(letters?|quick spark|slow simmer|nuanced|explicit|attuned)\b|\bwhat (is|are|does) (a |my |the )?wave ?codes?( mean)?\b|\b(quick spark|slow simmer)\b
what: Your Wave Code is four letters from Wavelength, one for each part. It’s a bit like the four-letter personality types you may have seen, but it’s a fun way to describe your preferences, not a test that measures you. Everyone uses both ends of each line sometimes.
Here’s what each letter means:
how: Q, Quick Spark (pace): you think fast and out loud, and ideas show up mid-sentence. The gift is energy and momentum. To tune in to a Q: let them think aloud without treating every idea as a final answer.

S, Slow Simmer (pace): you process inside before speaking, and the good thoughts often arrive later. The gift is depth and steadiness. To tune in to an S: give a heads-up before big talks, and accept “I need time to think” as a real answer.
F, Forest (lens): you see the big picture first: patterns, purpose and how it all connects. The gift is vision. To tune in to an F: start with the why, then help with the steps.
T, Trees (lens): you start with the specifics: steps, facts and exact details. The gift is precision and follow-through. To tune in to a T: be concrete. “Saturday at 10” beats “sometime soon.”
D, Direct (sending): you say it plainly, and honesty is how you show respect. The gift is clarity. To tune in to a D: listen to the words, not an imagined tone. Bluntness usually isn’t anger.
N, Nuanced (sending): you cushion what you say and read the moment, and may hint first. The gift is tact and warmth. To tune in to an N: make it safe to be direct, and take soft hints seriously.
E, Explicit (receiving): you take words at face value and want things spelled out. The gift is clear agreements. To tune in to an E: say exactly what you mean, without counting on hints or sarcasm.
A, Attuned (receiving): you read tone, mood and what’s under the words. The gift is empathy. To tune in to an A: mind your tone, and say so when you’re stressed about something else.

what: In Wavelength, the wiring step is optional, and you can select all that apply: Neurotypical, ADHD, Autistic, Dyslexic, Highly sensitive, Not sure yet, or Something else (with a box to name it). ADHD and Autistic together is often called AuDHD, and Wavelength says so. Your wiring only decides which options you see first in each part, and “Show options from other wiring types” opens the rest.

It’s self-identified, so no diagnosis is needed, and Wavelength is not a diagnosis or a test that measures you. If you’re not sure, the “Not sure which fits?” guide explains each type, with “you might relate if” examples and a “That’s me” button. If you’re curious about a formal assessment, a doctor or psychologist can help.
how: Open Wavelength and tap Start. The wiring step comes first.
Tap every type that fits you, or skip it. Picking “Not sure yet” shows options from every type.
Read the short explanation under your picks, or the guide below them if you need help.
Change it anytime with “Change my wiring” on your results.

cards.name: the 9 inputs of learning
cards.pat: \b(nine|9) inputs\b|\binputs? of learning\b|\blearning inputs?\b|\binputs?\b[^?]*\bwavelength\b|\bwavelength\b[^?]*\binputs?\b|\bstrongest input\b
what: The 9 inputs of learning are the ways people take in the world and make things click. Wavelength asks you to tap every one that helps you, then pick your strongest. They’re adapted from Howard Gardner’s idea of multiple intelligences. Treat them as preferences, not fixed learning styles: research doesn’t support learning through only one style, and most people learn best when several work together.
Here are the nine:
how: 💬 Words: talking, reading, writing and stories.
🔢 Logic and numbers: reasons, rules, numbers and how things work.
🖼️ Pictures and space: images, diagrams, color, maps and where things are.
🤲 Hands and movement: doing, touching, moving and making.
🎵 Sound and rhythm: tone, music, rhythm and how things sound.
🤝 People: learning with others and reading how they feel.
🌙 Inner reflection: quiet thinking, journaling and knowing yourself.
🌿 Nature and patterns: noticing, sorting and reading environments.
✨ Big questions and meaning: purpose, values and the why behind everything.
cards.pillar: Each input has its own self-discovery chapter, and “How the 9 inputs connect” maps their links in five levels, from obvious (words and people: conversation) to the deepest (hands and people: care sent through actions often goes unseen by a words-first partner), with three flowcharts and a nine-point check before a hard conversation.

what: To compare in Wavelength, the other person takes it too (on their own device, so their answers stay theirs) and tells you their four-letter Wave Code. On your results, type it under “Compare with someone.” You’ll see both archetypes, how many letters you share, and a tip for each of the four lines: pace, lens, sending and receiving.

Q and S: the Quick Spark can say “I’m just brainstorming,” and the Slow Simmer can say “I’ll come back to this by tonight.”
F and T: start with the big picture, then agree on the first concrete step together.
D and N: agree that plain words aren’t anger, and soft words still count.
E and A: say what you mean, and say it kindly. Here, both matter.

cards.name: the Lemonade Stand
cards.what: The Lemonade Stand is a free tool for seeing the work of keeping life running. It starts by asking who it’s for. “Just me” shows your own week as a ledger: where your time and attention go, the thinking work nobody sees, your rest, whether the week looks sustainable or stretched, and what you could hand off, drop, simplify or schedule, with a summary to explain your load to others. “Me and others I share a home with” works for two to eight people: partners, roommates, family or a small team. You list the week’s jobs and each person’s time (and, if you like, shared bills), and the split shows up as a plain fact, not a verdict on anyone. A built-in task library, from dishes to remembering birthdays, makes the list quick.
how: Pick who it’s for: “Just me” to see your own load, or “Me and others” for two to eight people who share a home. You can switch any time, and your entries stay.
If you share a home, add everyone’s names. Each person fills in only their own side.

Tap tasks in the task library (home, food, laundry, kids and caring, pets, money, admin, errands, planning and remembering, emotional work, work hours, rest and more). Typical minutes are filled in; change them to fit your week, or add your own jobs.
For each job, set how often it happens. Open “More” to add the thinking part (noticing, planning, remembering) and who notices first. The “who did what” log (WP-01) is the best source.
Optionally, add shared costs on the money side: what each person actually paid.
Look at the result calmly: the split or your own ledger, by area, the work you can and can’t see, and week by week if you save each week. Copy, print or share a clean summary if that helps.
Next step: give each job one owner with WP-03, and use the totals in CALC-01.
cards.results: The result shows each person’s share of the hours (and money, if you added it). An even split isn’t the goal in itself: what matters is whether everyone sees the same picture and agrees the split works. A lopsided split is a fact about the setup, often jobs that quietly drifted to whoever notices first, never a judgment of anyone.
cards.math: Each person’s share is their hours divided by everyone’s total hours. For two people, CALC-01 turns that into workload balance: 1 minus the difference between the two percentages, divided by 100, so an even split is 1.00 and a completely one-sided week is 0.00. With more people, the tool works the balance out from everyone’s hours for you.
cards.ex: Three roommates listed 14 jobs. The split came out 52%, 30% and 18%, mostly because one person always bought the shared groceries and cleaned the bathroom. They gave those two jobs new owners, and the next month it was much closer.
cards.pillar: Pillar I, See the whole load, with a nod to Pillar V, Notice the quiet incentives.

cards.name: WP-01, Who did what (the Field Audit)
cards.what: WP-01 is a one-week log of who did what at home, plus kind ways to say no. It catches what actually happened before memory turns the week into a story. It’s the usual first worksheet in the program.
how: For seven days, each of you logs your own tasks: the day, what it was, who did it, rough minutes, and whether someone asked or it was just noticed and handled.
Log the small and invisible jobs too, like noticing the milk is low.
Log what happened, not what should have: one honest row per task.
Don’t discuss it until the week is done. Then compare, calmly, or put the totals into the Lemonade Stand.
For saying no: say why the request is fair, say honestly what you have left, then offer something instead.
cards.results: WP-01 doesn’t give a score. It gives you both the same facts: total minutes per person, and how much was noticed versus asked for. Those totals feed the Lemonade Stand and CALC-01’s workload balance.
cards.ex: “Tuesday, noticed we’re out of dish soap, bought it on the way home, 15 min, noticed (not asked).” That one row is the invisible work WP-01 is designed to catch.
start: Pick a start day, like tomorrow morning.
Keep the log somewhere easy: the fill-in version on screen, a printed sheet, or your phone’s notes.
Log just your own side for seven days, small jobs included, and don’t compare until the week is done.
cards.pillar: Pillar I, See the whole load. Its kind ways to say no use Pillar IV.

cards.name: WP-02, the Battery & Stress Meter
cards.what: WP-02 is a quick, kind check on yourself that separates how much you’re already carrying from how upset you are about one thing. Sometimes a small thing feels huge because the rest of the day was heavy. It’s a gut-check, not a medical test.
how: Fill it in only about yourself, thinking about the last day or two.
Score five things from 0 (not at all) to 4 (very true): sleep, workload elsewhere, any unresolved conflict, how your body feels, and time pressure today.
Add them up and divide by 20.
Use the result to pace a hard talk, not to dodge one. You can also type your five answers to me and I’ll work it out.
cards.results: Under 0.3: whatever comes up is probably about the thing itself. From 0.3 to 0.6: say out loud, “Heads up, I’m carrying more than usual today.” Over 0.6: be gentle with yourself and put off anything that doesn’t need deciding in the next hour. A high score means “later”, not “never”. It describes your state today, not a verdict on you.
cards.math: Five answers, each 0 to 4, so the most you can score is 20. Add them up and divide by 20 to get a number from 0 to 1. For example, 3 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 12, and 12 ÷ 20 = 0.60. In CALC-01, the average of everyone’s battery scores becomes the stress input, and it goes in flipped, as (1 − the score), so more stress lowers the read.
cards.ex: Answers of 3, 2, 4, 1 and 2 add up to 12, and 12 ÷ 20 = 0.60, the top of the middle band: a good day to say “Heads up, I’m carrying more than usual today” before anything hard.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.
links: WP-02: How full is your battery?

cards.name: WP-03, One owner per job (the RACI Treaty)
cards.what: WP-03 gives every regular job one clear owner, so nobody has to keep asking and nothing is left vaguely shared. It works for two people or a group (it’s the same idea teams use, called RACI).
how: Sit down once, ideally with a week of the WP-01 log.
List the regular jobs: groceries, dishes, bills, the family calendar, and your own.
For each, write how often it happens and two names: the Responsible person (does it) and the Accountable person (notices if it didn’t get done). They can be the same person.
Agree on it together. Agreeing means clear, not perfect.
Change it on purpose at the weekly closing, never by drift.
cards.results: Count the jobs with both names filled in and divide by the total number of jobs. That’s your ownership clarity, from 0 to 1. Keep unowned jobs on the list: seeing them is the whole point. Higher clarity means fewer “I thought you were doing it” moments.
cards.math: Ownership clarity = jobs with both a Responsible and an Accountable name ÷ all jobs listed. Eight fully owned jobs out of ten gives 0.80. It measures how clear ownership is, not how fair it is, and it feeds CALC-01 with a weight of 0.35.
cards.ex: “Bins: weekly, Responsible Jordan, Accountable Jordan.” “Dentist appointments: as needed, Responsible Sam, Accountable Sam.” Two rows, and two jobs nobody has to ask about again.
cards.pillar: Pillar II, Fix the setup, not the person, with a nod to Pillar V.

cards.name: WP-04, What keeps coming back? (the Deficit Audit)
cards.what: WP-04 is a gentle monthly look back, done together, to find the jobs that keep slipping and fix the setup instead of patching the same problem again.
how: Once a month, bring your four weekly WP-01 logs and your WP-03 job list.
List every job that was noticed but not done, or only done after being raised more than once. Check off each week it happened.
Three or four checks is a pattern, not a fluke.
Sort each repeat: no clear owner (update WP-03), the owner can’t keep up (a kind, honest talk), or a temporary cause like illness or travel (note it and move on).
Make the changes, and write down how many structural gaps you found.
cards.results: The number to watch is structural gaps: jobs with no clear owner. Fewer each month means it’s working. More means the setup needs another look, not that anyone failed.
cards.pillar: Pillar II, Fix the setup, not the person, with a nod to Pillar V.

cards.name: WP-09, Say it so it lands (the Tone Filter)
cards.what: WP-09 is a quick self-check to run before you answer something that stung, so what you say is something the other person can actually hear. It only looks at your own next message.
how: Before you speak, find three things: the fact, in one sentence with no adjectives; the feeling underneath, like tired or unseen; and the ask, what you want to happen next.
If your sentence is a judgment on the person (“you always…”), swap it for one fact and one ask.
Before you react, weigh what you heard: is it about a specific task? Would it read the same if you weren’t stretched? Could a neutral meaning fit?
If you’re stretched or unsure, pause first.
cards.results: There’s no score. The result is a better sentence. In CALC-01, the share of friction moments you ran through fact, feeling and ask becomes retuning frequency, which feeds the apex score.
cards.ex: “You never think about anyone but yourself” becomes: “The bin wasn’t out before pickup. I feel a bit unseen. Can we pick a fixed day for it?”
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.
links: WP-09: Say it so it lands

cards.name: WP-11, the Calm-Down Kit
cards.what: WP-11 is a plan you make while calm for bringing your body back down in a heated moment, so you can finish the conversation or honestly put it off. It’s for you, never something to hand to the other person.
how: On an ordinary, calm day, write what tends to set you off and where you feel it first.
Pick two calming steps (like breathing in for four and out for six, or a slow walk).
Write one pause line: how you feel, how long, when you’ll be back.
In the moment: check your battery, say your line, do your first calming step.
Check your battery again before going back.
cards.results: It uses your WP-02 battery score to decide when to go back: under 0.50, go back at the time you said; between 0.50 and 0.60, do another round; still 0.60 or more after two rounds, pick a new time and say when. When you go back, start with one small, simple task first.
cards.ex: A pause line: “I’m getting too wound up to listen well. I’m going for a ten-minute walk, and I’ll be back at 7:30 to finish this.”
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: WP-13, the 90-second daily check-in
cards.what: WP-13 is a 90-second daily check-in that makes small corrections every day, so little things don’t pile up into a big weekend argument. Small and often beats big and rare.
how: Pick a regular moment, like after dinner.

Each of you says one sentence each on: how full you were today (low, medium or high), one thing you appreciated about the other, and optionally one small thing that didn’t feel great and one thing that would help tomorrow.
One speaks, the other just listens. No debating, and nothing gets solved here.
Once a week, skim the notes: anything that came up more than twice moves to WP-03 or WP-09.
cards.results: No score. The sign it’s working is fewer surprises: small things get mentioned while they’re small, and a daily thank-you keeps things steady.
cards.ex: “Medium today. I appreciated you handling the vet call. The sink pile got to me a bit. Tomorrow it’d help if we did the dishes right after dinner.” That’s the whole thing, about 30 seconds.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive, with a nod to Pillar V.

cards.name: CALC-01, Can the load last? (the Solvency Read)
cards.what: CALC-01 gives one read on whether the way you share the work right now can keep going. It scores the setup, never a person, and it isn’t a compatibility test. There’s a quick three-slider version and a full version that works each input out from your worksheets and keeps a trend log. It works for households and teams of two to eight people.
how: Before reading any number, check your own state (Step Zero).
Workload balance: enter the week’s hours per person from WP-01 or the Lemonade Stand.
Ownership clarity: list the regular jobs from WP-03 and who is Responsible and Accountable for each.
Battery: each person enters their own five WP-02 answers, about themselves only.
Optionally, count friction moments and how many you retuned with WP-09 (for the apex score).
Read the result together, calmly, and look at the biggest shortfall first.
cards.results: 0.70 or more: the setup is carrying its own weight, so keep the same rhythm of check-ins. 0.40 to 0.69: something is drifting; look at the input with the biggest gap (often ownership clarity, but check). Under 0.40: the setup can’t last as it is, so rework the whole agreement rather than patching. The band edges are round numbers: 0.69 and 0.70 are really the same week. It’s a starting point, not a verdict.
cards.math: Solvency = 0.40 × workload balance + 0.35 × ownership clarity + 0.25 × (1 − average battery score). Each input runs from 0 to 1, so the read does too. The battery goes in flipped, because a setup that only works when everyone is well rested isn’t working. The apex score adds repair: 0.35 × balance + 0.30 × ownership + 0.20 × (1 − battery) + 0.15 × retuning frequency. The weights are an openly stated judgment call, not numbers fitted to data. For exact details (and how it handles more than two people), the full CALC-01 page shows every formula.
cards.ex: Balance 0.60, ownership 0.50 and battery 0.40 give 0.40 × 0.60 + 0.35 × 0.50 + 0.25 × 0.60 = 0.24 + 0.175 + 0.15 = 0.57: something is drifting, and ownership has the biggest gap. You can type your own numbers to me, like “CALC-01: balance 0.6, ownership 0.5, battery 0.4”.
cards.pillar: Pillar I, See the whole load, and Pillar II, Fix the setup, not the person. Step Zero uses Pillar III.
links: Chapter II: Is the split working?

cards.name: REPORT-01, Your progress, week by week (the Full Read)
cards.what: REPORT-01 is one place to type in what your worksheets produced each week, and a report that reads them side by side to show where they agree and where they don’t. It brings all Five Pillars together, and reads the setup, never a person.
how: Once a week, after your short end-of-week review, copy in the figures from the worksheets you ran: WP-01 minutes, WP-02 scores, WP-03 counts and so on. Leave blank what you didn’t run.
Once a month, add your WP-04 look-back: the gaps you found, and how many came back after being fixed.
Press Save ledger to download a small file, and Load ledger next week to carry on. Nothing is stored in the browser or sent anywhere.
cards.results: The report says where things stand, how the numbers fit together, and what to do next, following written rules you can check. The repeat count from the monthly look-back matters most: problems that come back after being fixed point to the setup.
cards.pillar: All Five Pillars together.

cards.name: PROG-01, Six gentle weeks
cards.what: PROG-01 is a six-week path through the program, one step at a time. It works best with the other person, but you can do it on your own.
how: Week 1, see the work: read the Preface and Chapter I, check your state with Today’s Weather, and log a week in WP-01.
Week 2, one owner per job: read Chapter II, fill in WP-03, and get a first read from CALC-01.
Week 3, your batteries: read Chapters III and IV, and do the WP-02 Battery Meter daily.
Week 4, talk about it kindly: WP-09 and your Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).
Week 5, get back in step: the 90-second daily check-in (WP-13).
Week 6, make it last: log another week, compare with week one, and do your first monthly look-back (WP-04).
cards.pillar: All Five Pillars, in order.
links: The curriculum (the order, week by week)

cards.name: the Workpaper Suite
cards.what: The Workpaper Suite lines up the workpapers for your road in the order that helps most. Pick who it’s for (just you, partners, family, co-parents, friends, roommates, coworkers, caregivers, or the 6-week program), fill the sheets in on screen, then download one fillable PDF and a report written for your road.
how: Choose your road, and optionally add the first names of the people on it (they appear in every owner drop-down).
Work through your road by step, or week by week.
Bring in anything you’ve already filled in: draft files, a suite file, or a fillable PDF.
Download the fillable PDF to type into on your phone or print, and the report for your road.
Save a suite file to pick up next time, even on another device.
cards.results: The report tells your road’s story from what you wrote: where things stand, a question to talk about for each sheet, what to look for, conversation starters, your weeks, and kind words worth keeping close.
cards.more: Each road has its own order. Partners start with who did what (WP-01), then one owner per job (WP-03), batteries (WP-02), talking so it lands (WP-09 and WP-11), the daily check-in (WP-13) and the monthly look-back (WP-04). Just you starts with your battery, what settles you, and how words reach you. Roommates and coworkers lean on the Lemonade Stand and one owner per job. The whole road, every sheet in order, comes out as one fillable PDF plus the report: that’s the full-path package.
cards.pillar: Every road uses all Five Pillars, starting inside you and then between you and others.
links: Fill in one workpaper at a time

cards.name: the full-path package
cards.what: The full-path package is the Workpaper Suite’s way of giving you your whole road in one go: every workpaper on your road, in order, as one fillable PDF, plus a report written from what you filled in.
how: Open the Workpaper Suite and choose your road.
Fill in what you can on screen, or bring in drafts and PDFs you’ve already filled in.
Download the fillable PDF (every sheet on your road, ready to type into or print) and the report.
Save a suite file if you want to pick it up later.
cards.pillar: All Five Pillars, in your road’s order.

cards.name: the fill-in workpapers
cards.what: Every workpaper has a fill-in version: type your entries on screen and download a finished PDF to keep. Nothing is stored unless you turn on “Keep a draft on this device”, and you can erase it any time.
how: Open the fill-in page and pick a workpaper (the usual order is WP-01, WP-02, WP-03, WP-09, WP-11 and WP-13, with WP-04 once a month).
Type your entries.
Download the PDF, or keep a draft on this device if it’s your own device.
Or do them all at once, in your road’s order, in the Workpaper Suite.
cards.pillar: Each workpaper names its own pillar.

cards.name: the Workpaper Playground
cards.what: The Workpaper Playground lets you try three core tools in a few minutes, with real calculations and nothing saved: WP-01 (who’s doing what), WP-03 (one owner per job) and CALC-01 (can the load last).
how: Open the Playground.
Try a quick week in WP-01, a few jobs in WP-03, and see how they feed CALC-01.
When it clicks, move to the real fill-in workpapers or the Workpaper Suite.
cards.pillar: Pillar I, See the whole load, and Pillar II, Fix the setup, not the person.

cards.name: Today’s Weather
cards.what: Today’s Weather is a free, one-minute reading of your own conditions today: the sky, the pressure, the ground underneath, and what’s blowing in. It tells you what today is good for, and what to leave until the front moves through. It’s a reading of you, never of anyone else.
how: Step 1 (the only required one): pick the sky closest to true right now: Clear (calm and connected), Gusty (revved up) or Fogged in (running on empty).
Optionally add who you’ll be around, how much you were already carrying, body needs, last night’s sleep, people load, what’s on your mind, and what would help in the next hour.
Read your forecast: good hours for, what to leave for later, a talk window, and sixty seconds that might help.
Keep a private almanac on your device if you’d like to spot patterns.
cards.results: The forecast is a rough tally of what you told it, not a measurement. The sky sets the starting point, and heavy pressure, a short night, lots of people time, body needs and open worries each add a little. A closed talk window means “not now”, never “never”. Weather isn’t a grade or a diagnosis: conditions pass.
cards.ex: Gusty sky, heavy pressure and a short night might give you: good hours for simple tasks and a walk; leave the budget talk until tomorrow; say “I’m running low today, can we talk tomorrow?”
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.
links: WP-02: How full is your battery?

cards.name: the 2-minute Snapshot
cards.what: The Snapshot is seven quick questions about how a shared load is set up, and how it bends when things get heavy. It shows which of four areas you’re in right now, what’s shaping it, and one small step for this week. It looks through all Five Pillars.
how: Pick who shares the load with you (partner, family, roommates, shared care, a team, someone else).
Answer the seven questions honestly, for today.
Read your area and the one thing to try this week.
It works best when each person takes it on their own, then you compare.
cards.results: Four areas: Steady (clear setup, bends well), Ready to readjust (blurry setup, bends well), Stuck pattern (clear setup, hard to bend) and Stretched thin (blurry setup, hard to bend). It’s one moment from one point of view, not a verdict, so try it again in a month.
cards.pillar: All Five Pillars: questions 1 to 3 look at the setup (Pillars I and II), 4 to 6 at how it bends (III, IV and V).

cards.name: the Wiring Card
cards.what: The Wiring Card is a one-page card on how you actually receive words: what silence means for you, what helps, and what to avoid. You give it to people you live or work with before a hard conversation, not during one. It isn’t a diagnosis, a label or a contract, and nothing you type is saved.
how: On a calm day, fill in how you take in words, pace and tone. The card updates as you go.
Print or copy it.
Give it to the people you live and work with, before a hard conversation.
Pair it with the Signal Translator to test a sentence, and with Check-ins when the topic needs a calm space.
cards.results: The card tells someone how to send a request so it gets through. It doesn’t make them responsible for managing you, and it doesn’t mean you must be available however you feel. When you’re running low, every line applies more strictly.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: the Signal Translator
cards.what: The Signal Translator lets you type what you plan to say or send, see how it may land, and get a clearer version that keeps your ask. Everything besides the sentence is optional.
how: Type your sentence the way it would really come out: a text, a Slack message, or something you’ll say out loud.
Optionally pick the relationship, the channel, the listener’s wiring and state, and the situation.
Press Translate to see how it may land and a clearer version.
Try the reverse to see how you might read their reply.
Add sentences to your talking notes and print them for a check-in.
cards.results: It shows how the sentence may land for that listener, what might sting, and a clearer version with the same ask. It’s a guide, not a verdict on your words or on them. Acknowledgement isn’t agreement, and hearing how it landed doesn’t cancel your fact.
cards.ex: “You never help with the kids’ stuff” might come back as: “The school forms were due today and I did them last night. I felt stretched. Could you take the forms from now on?”
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.
links: WP-09: Say it so it lands

cards.name: the Carrier Wave Decoder
cards.what: The Carrier Wave Decoder is a guided session for the moment a conversation starts going sideways, with anyone. You work out what was out of sync, check your state, retune your body, practice with a guided script, and keep notes on what works. It puts Chapter I’s radio idea into practice.
how: Start a session and pick the state closest to how you feel: calm, revved up, or shut down.
Decode the moment: for pace, tone and timing, mark where you were and your best guess at where they were.
Do a one-minute retune (a long exhale if you’re keyed up, looking around if you’ve gone flat).
Practice a no-blame sentence, then run a private tone check on your draft before you send it.
Save what worked to your journal on this device.
cards.results: It shows which channel slipped out of sync (pace, tone or timing) and gives you a way to name it without blame. It isn’t a verdict on who was right. Save anything hard for a planned check-in.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive; the state check uses Pillar III.
links: Chapter I: Why we get out of tune

cards.name: the Conversation Reader
cards.what: The Conversation Reader lets you paste a text thread, chat or email exchange and see where it turned, what each of you may be hearing, and a calmer way to answer. It runs entirely in your browser: what you paste is never saved or sent.
how: Copy the messages from your phone, chat app or email and paste them in. Names at the start of lines help but aren’t required.
Tell it which person is you, if there are names.
Read where it got heated and what each of you may be hearing.
Write your reply, and let the Reader check it as you type before you send.
cards.results: It looks for patterns in words (absolutes like “always” and “never”, sentences about who someone is, dismissals, sarcasm, repair attempts, clear asks, unanswered questions) and weighs them to show where it heated up. It can’t hear tone of voice or know your history, so use it to slow down and prepare, never as proof of who was right.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: Frequency Calibration
cards.what: Frequency Calibration maps the natural rhythms two people run on across five areas (money, rest and recovery, decisions, talking, and big-picture values), shows where you’re out of step, and suggests simple shared habits to get back in line. It isn’t a diagnosis or a compatibility test.
how: First choose who it’s for: “Just me” maps your own rhythms and how to plan around them and explain them; “Me and someone close to me” compares two people’s rhythms.
For two people, add both names (optional) and how you’re connected.
Person A picks what feels natural in each area; then Person B does the same.
Compare your rhythms to see the gap in each area.
Try one agreement at a time, starting with the biggest gap, for two weeks before judging it.
Run it again every few months as life changes.
cards.results: Each gap is how many steps apart your answers are. A big gap doesn’t mean anyone is wrong: you’re running at different speeds, and a shared agreement usually closes most of it. Agreement you schedule tends to hold better than agreement you assume.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive, with a nod to Pillar III.

cards.name: the Frequency Sync Visualizer
cards.what: The Frequency Sync Visualizer is a moving picture of two rhythms, yours and another person’s. When they drift apart, the picture gets choppy; tap “Check in” and they settle into step, the way the 90-second daily check-in does. It’s a picture of an idea, not a measurement of anyone.
how: Set your rhythm and theirs (beats a second).
Watch the gap, and bring them closer or tap Check in.
Turn sound on with headphones to hear each rhythm in one ear.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: Mood Arbitrage
cards.what: Mood Arbitrage is about noticing the state someone’s body is in and gently helping a tense moment soften, starting with calming your own body first. It isn’t forced cheerfulness. The free introduction shows the core idea and one full example; the full toolkit adds five everyday scenarios, 15-plus ready-made moves and a four-week practice plan.
how: Start with the free introduction and its worked example.
Notice the state first: calm, revved up or shut down.
Settle your own body before anything else.
Choose one small move or phrase that fits their state, like a circuit breaker.
Then open the full toolkit for the scenarios and the four-week plan.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first, and Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: Drift, the calm visualizer
cards.what: Drift is a quiet few minutes for your senses. You tell it how you feel, and it picks a soft pair of tones, a slow breathing pace and deep, dreamy 3D colors to match, then eases everything toward calmer over the first few minutes. Everything is made on your device.
how: Put headphones on (binaural tones only work with headphones), and start the volume low.
Pick the feeling closest to how you are, how strong it is, and how long you’d like (about 5 to 20 minutes).
Choose pictures, background sound and breathing words, or gentle, nearly still visuals.
Press Begin, and just breathe along. Stop anytime if it doesn’t feel good.
Not while driving or doing anything that needs your full attention.
cards.results: At the end it asks how you feel now. Noticing how you feel before and after is Pillar III in action, and a settled moment is a kinder time for a talk you’ve been saving. It’s a relaxing experience, not a treatment.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: the Night Garden
cards.what: The Night Garden is a calm place to breathe, play and let your mind settle. There are no timers and no way to lose, and it keeps growing as you visit.
how: Breathe: box breathing with a glowing light (in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4); a flower blooms with every round.
Fireflies: connect stars into singing constellations and dedicate each one to someone you love (kept on this device only).
Lily pond: a slow, gentle puzzle where lily pads bloom as you fit them into rows.
Switch between them anytime; headphones are lovely here.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: Pause & Play
cards.what: Pause & Play is the calm corner of the site: gentle games for when your mind needs a rest. Drift, the Night Garden, Tidbit and Sugarfoot’s Arcade, Word Bloom, Quiet Crossword, the Daily Ledger Crossword and Quiet Words. No timers, no way to lose, and every few levels something new appears in the living garden behind every page.
how: Pick a game that fits your mood: breathing (Night Garden, Drift), words (Word Bloom, Quiet Words, the crosswords) or a quick arcade round (Tidbit and Sugarfoot’s Arcade).
Play a few minutes to settle before a hard conversation, or to wind down at night.
Your level and streak are kept on this device only.
cards.pillar: Mostly Pillar III, Read your state first: settle, then talk.

cards.name: Word Bloom
cards.what: Word Bloom is a calm word game: swipe across the petals to spell words and fill a little crossword. Other real words go in your bonus jar. There are hundreds of gentle levels, no timer and no way to lose.
how: Drag your finger from petal to petal to spell a word, then let go. Slide back to undo a letter.
Or tap petals one at a time and tap the middle, or type on a keyboard.
The shuffle button mixes up the letters and the hint button shows one letter.
Finish a level without hints for a perfect bloom.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first: one gentle thing to hold.

cards.name: the Quiet Crossword
cards.what: The Quiet Crossword is a small, friendly crossword made for playing on a phone, from gentle to expert. Each word glows when it’s right, and there’s no timer.
how: Tap a square and type; tap again to switch between across and down.
Use “Check my letters” or “Show a letter” whenever you like.
Play the next one, or pick a random one.
cards.pillar: Pillar III: a small puzzle gives your mind one gentle thing to hold.

cards.name: the Daily Ledger Crossword
cards.what: The Daily Ledger Crossword is a real newspaper-style crossword, from a quick 5×5 Mini to a Big Sunday 13×13. The grids grow bigger and the clues a little trickier as you go, and there’s still no timer.
how: Tap a square and type; tap it again to switch between across and down.
The small numbers match the clues. Some squares belong to only one word, as in British newspaper crosswords.
The short, one-word clues are the trickier ones.
cards.pillar: Pillar III: a calm puzzle before or after a busy day.

cards.name: Quiet Words
cards.what: Quiet Words is a gentle word search with a new theme in every puzzle. There’s no timer, no score and no way to lose. Each word you find glows, rings softly and leaves a kind thought behind.
how: Choose a theme, or take the next puzzle.
Find the words at your own pace; “Show me a letter” helps if you’re stuck.
Notice each word, and the thought it leaves behind.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: Tidbit and Sugarfoot’s Arcade
cards.what: Tidbit and Sugarfoot’s Arcade (on Tidbit and Sugarfoot’s Arcade page) is a little arcade with two best friends, Tidbit and Sugarfoot. Pick which pup to play as, then pick one of five gentle classic games: Treat Chase (a maze where a golden heart turns the grumpy Static into bubbles you can pop), Cross the Way (hop over a road and ride logs across a river to five doghouses), The Treat Trail (a wagon-trail journey from Puddle Hollow to Starfall Hill: choose your pace and snack sizes, cross rivers, trade at posts), Bubble Break (a brick breaker) and Treat Shower (catch falling treats in a basket). Every level after the first is new, and there’s no game over: run low on treats and you forage, run low on energy and you rest.
how: Pick Tidbit or Sugarfoot, pick one of the five games, and press Start.

Steer with the arrow keys or WASD, a swipe, a tap on the playfield, or the big on-screen arrows. In Bubble Break and Treat Shower you can also drag; in The Treat Trail you tap a choice or press its number. A turn you press a little early is remembered.
Relaxed pace (on by default) slows everything down. Pause any time.
Each level you clear counts toward the garden behind every page.
cards.more: Tidbit is a little quicker; Sugarfoot is steadier, her golden hearts last longer and she’s harder to bump. Each new level brings a fresh maze, shuffled lanes, new hedges or a new wall, and a line of kindness you won’t see twice until you’ve seen them all. On the same page you can open the pal cam and watch Frequency Buddies.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive, while you settle with Pillar III.

cards.name: the pal cam
keys: check in on tidbit and sugarfoot
see what they re up to
what are tidbit and sugarfoot doing
cards.what: The pal cam is a little full-screen window on the Frequency Journey page (Tidbit and Sugarfoot’s Arcade) and the home page, where you can check in on Tidbit and Sugarfoot and see what they’re up to. They act out small scripted activities, the setting changes each time you open it, and the light follows your own clock.
how: Open Tidbit and Sugarfoot’s Arcade page.
Tap “Check in on Tidbit & Sugarfoot”.
Watch for a while; close it whenever you like. The tally of what they’ve done today stays in this browser only.
cards.pillar: A calm moment with the pals: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: Soundscapes: Brain Breakers
cards.what: The Soundscapes page is now all about Brain Breakers: four instrumental pieces by Christian’s Lab, each with a different job. Shooting Star is the softest and most floating, for quieting a busy mind, anxiety or pre-sleep wind-down. Thunderous Shimmer is textural and restless, for recovery that needs a spark and a little curious alertness. Watching a Shooting Star is the most expansive and cinematic, for shifting out of a stuck or low-energy state. Bouncy Bedroom is short, intimate and playful (alternative R&B, Chicago bounce and bedroom-pop), for lifting low energy or mild boredom with a small bounce while staying relaxed. The page also has See and feel the sound, and a short picker. These are listening notes, not a clinical tool.
how: Open Soundscapes and tap what you need in Find your Brain Breaker, or just press play on a track.
Press See and feel this to watch the track and, on an Android phone with Chrome, feel it as vibration.
Headphones help, and start with the volume low.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: Echoes of Gold
cards.what: Echoes of Gold is the companion album: 11 songs (about 41 minutes) that Christian made, performing as Loves Journey, before The Objective Ledger had a single worksheet. The workpapers make the practical side easy to read; the album carries what the numbers were never going to reach.
how: Listen on Spotify or Apple Music from the album page.
Use it for settling first (Pillar III), before a talk or at the end of the day.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: the podcast
cards.what: The Kane and Christian Experience explores the program through stories, real-life examples and conversation. Each episode dives into one workpaper, chapter or theme; listen in any order or follow the path matched to the PROG-01 weeks. No episodes are published yet: the first three are recorded and coming soon, and the rest are in production or planned.
how: Open the podcast page and filter by theme (foundation, diagnostics, communication, resonance).
When episodes are out, start with Episode 1 on Unbilled Debt, or pick the one matching your current week.
cards.pillar: Each episode names its chapter or workpaper, and so its pillar.

cards.name: Turning Toward
cards.what: Turning Toward is a guide to seven small, everyday ways to build connection with anyone who matters to you: a partner, a friend, family, a roommate or a coworker. Closeness is built mostly in tiny moments, like a joke, a sigh or a “look at this”, and in how you answer them.
how: Try today’s small moment (a new idea appears each day), like saying one specific thank-you.
Pick who it’s for, copy the message if you like, and change anything in [brackets] to fit.
Notice when someone reaches for you, and reach back, even briefly.
Track your week of small moments on your device.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive, and Pillar V, Notice the quiet incentives.

cards.name: the Check-ins guide
cards.what: A check-in is a short, agreed talk about one hard topic, at a time that works for both of you. The Check-ins guide covers picking a good moment, the ground rules (one topic, same side), hearing it back before you answer, and ending well.
how: Agree on a time, not the middle of a stressful moment: private, phones down, nobody hungry.
Open with: “I’m not against you. I don’t think you meant harm. I want to sort out this one thing.”
One person says one fact and how it landed; the other says back what they heard and asks, “Did I get that?” Then swap.
If either of you gets too wound up or flat, pause and name a time to come back.
End with one ask, one owner, one time.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first, and Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: Know your own wiring
cards.what: Know your own wiring helps with “why do I react this way?”. Most reactions come from three places at once: your wiring (how you’re built, which stays), patterns life has taught you (which can shift with practice), and today’s conditions (sleep, stress, load, which pass). Knowing which is which helps you understand yourself and explain yourself to others.
how: Think of a recent reaction that surprised you.
Sort it: how much was wiring, how much a learned pattern, how much today’s conditions?
Work on what can change, plan around what stays, and go easy on yourself about what’s just today.
Tell people what’s lasting, what you’re working on and what today needs.
cards.pillar: Mainly Pillar III and Pillar IV, with help from Pillars I and II.

cards.name: Wired Differently
cards.what: Wired Differently explains how differently wired people hear the same words, and how to talk across the difference. A mix-up usually runs both ways, so it’s tuning, not anyone’s fault. The full guide walks through 14 wirings one by one, like highly sensitive people, autistic people, ADHD and people who find feelings hard to name.
how: Read the short version for the main ideas: the double empathy problem, sensitivity, and finding words for feelings.
Find the wirings that sound like you or someone close, in the full guide.
Make a Wiring Card, and test one sentence in the Signal Translator.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: the Five Pillars
cards.what: Everything in the program rests on five simple ideas. Each starts inside you, as a way to understand yourself, then shows up between you and the people you share life with. I, See the whole load. II, Fix the setup, not the person. III, Read your state first. IV, Tune how you send and receive. V, Notice the quiet incentives.
how: You see the load (I): notice everything you carry, then put it on one shared, fair page.
You redesign the setup around it (II): habits are a setup, not a character flaw; one owner per job instead of blame.
You check your state before you talk (III): calm, revved up or shut down; pick your timing.
You tune the message so it lands (IV): know your wiring, and translate across different wiring.
You watch for the quiet pulls that let things slide back (V): defaults, and how unclaimed jobs drift to one person.
cards.ex: Tuesday, 7 p.m., the sink is full again. You could say “you never help.” Or you could see everything you both did today (I), notice the dishes have no owner (II), check you’re too tired to talk well right now (III), say it later in a way that lands (IV), and notice that whoever sees the mess first has quietly become the one who always cleans it (V).
cards.pillar: They borrow, in order, from ledger accounting, systems thinking, nervous-system science, signal theory and behavioral economics.

cards.name: Pillar I, See the whole load
cards.what: Pillar I, See the whole load, borrows from ledger accounting. In you: notice everything you carry, including the invisible, mental and emotional load (remembering, planning, worrying, keeping the peace). Between you and others: put it on one shared, fair page, so nobody has to argue about whose work “counts”.
how: Log one week of who did what (WP-01).
Put it on the Lemonade Stand.
Read the Preface on the work nobody sees.

cards.name: Pillar II, Fix the setup, not the person
keys: fix the setup not the person
cards.what: Pillar II, Fix the setup, not the person, borrows from systems thinking. In you: see your habits and routines as a setup you can redesign, not a character flaw. Between you and others: clear owners, handoffs and agreements (one owner per job) instead of blame.
how: Give each regular job one owner (WP-03).
Once a month, look for what keeps coming back (WP-04).
Read Chapter II on whether the split is working.

cards.name: Pillar III, Read your state first
cards.what: Pillar III, Read your state first, borrows from nervous-system science. In you: know how full your battery is (calm, revved up or shut down) before you judge a moment. Between you and others: pick the timing, pause and come back; your state shapes how the other person’s words land.
how: Check Today’s Weather or your WP-02 battery before a hard talk.
Plan what settles you in the Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).
Read Chapter III on full tanks.

cards.name: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive
keys: tune how you send and receive
cards.what: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive, borrows from signal theory (the Frequency Framework). In you: know your own wiring, pace and how you hear things. Between you and others: translate across different wiring and tone; a mismatch is tuning, not a moral failing.
how: Make a Wiring Card.
Test a sentence in the Signal Translator, or use fact, feeling and ask (WP-09).
Read Chapter I on why we get out of tune.

cards.name: Pillar V, Notice the quiet incentives
cards.what: Pillar V, Notice the quiet incentives, borrows from behavioral economics. In you: spot the defaults and shortcuts that steer your own choices. Between you and others: see how unclaimed jobs drift to one person, and how fairness and thanks keep things steady.
how: Notice which jobs you do only because you notice first.
Say one specific thank-you a day (Turning Toward, WP-13).
Read Chapter IV on two kinds of fair and Chapter V on the monthly look-back.

cards.name: the Frequency Framework
cards.what: The Frequency Framework explains why two kind people can fall out of step: like two radios tuned to slightly different stations, small differences in pace, tone and urgency create a “squeal” neither person made alone. It’s tuning, not a character problem, and small regular check-ins bring you back in step.
how: Read the Frequency Framework and Chapter I.
Map your rhythms with Frequency Calibration.
Use the 90-second daily check-in (WP-13) as your shared rhythm.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: the Preface, The work nobody sees
cards.what: The Preface is about the work nobody sees: remembering appointments, noticing the milk is low, calming a tense moment. None of it shows up on a calendar, so it rarely gets a thank-you, and over months it piles up. The book calls that pile unbilled debt. It’s free to read.
how: Read the simple version first, then the full preface if you want the detail.
Try a week of WP-01 to see your own unbilled work.
Listen to podcast Episode 1 if you like a human voice with the ideas.
cards.pillar: Mostly Pillar I, See the whole load, with Pillar V.

cards.name: Chapter I, Why we get out of tune
keys: why we get out of tune
cards.what: Chapter I explains why two kind, reasonable people can end up in a tangle neither started, and how to get back in step. The tangle often isn’t about the words but the tone underneath: like two radios slightly out of tune, making a crackle neither makes alone. It’s free to read.
how: Read the simple version, then the full chapter.
Try the Carrier Wave Decoder the next time a conversation squeals.
cards.pillar: Mostly Pillar IV, with help from Pillar III.

cards.name: Chapter II, Is the split working?
cards.what: Chapter II asks one gentle question: can the way you share the work keep going, or is one of you quietly running on empty? It looks at the month, not last night, using what you both wrote down, and it introduces the three numbers behind CALC-01. It looks at the arrangement, never at a person. It’s free to read.
how: Read the chapter, then fill in WP-01 and WP-03.
Get a first read in CALC-01.
cards.pillar: Pillar I and Pillar II, with help from Pillar III.

cards.name: Chapter III, Full tanks and different angles
cards.what: Chapter III explains why some reactions are bigger than their cause (a full tank overflows) and why two people can see the same moment so differently: the seven angles people see things from. Anything decided while a tank is overflowing is worth coming back to. It opens free with your email.
how: Read the chapter, then try the WP-02 Battery Meter daily for a week.
Plan your pause in the Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).
cards.pillar: Mostly Pillar III, with help from Pillar IV.

cards.name: Chapter IV, Two kinds of fair
cards.what: Chapter IV is about agreeing what “fair” means before you argue about it, and giving a comment a moment to land before you answer. One kind of fair asks “did everything get done?”, the other “did each of us do what we said?”. Both are reasonable; friction starts when you’re each using a different one. It opens free with your email.
how: Talk about which kind of fair each of you uses, on a calm day.
Practice letting a comment land (WP-09) before you answer.
cards.pillar: Pillar II and Pillar V, with help from Pillar III.

cards.name: Chapter V, The monthly look-back
cards.what: Chapter V is about looking back once a month for the problems that keep coming back, and fixing the setup instead of having the same argument again. One missed job is a fluke; the same job missed four weeks running is a pattern you only see across the month. It opens free with your email.
how: Bring four weekly logs and your job list.
Run WP-04, the monthly look-back.

Every entry has the same parts: in a nutshell, going deeper, what the research says and its limits, how it connects to the program, and questions to talk about. It’s general education, not diagnosis or therapy.

Read one entry a day, or ask me “what is…” about any of them.

cards.name: the creator
cards.what: The program was made by Christian, who worked as a government auditor and audit manager and has spent a lifetime studying how people work: psychology, philosophy, neurobiology and more. He’s autistic, with ADHD, OCD and anxiety in the mix, and built the program from what he learned about his own wiring and about systems.

cards.name: the logo
cards.what: The logo is Peach and Lilac: one round and one a squishy square, because nobody is wired quite the same, sharing one heart between them. That’s the whole idea of Spread Love & Acceptance: see each other fairly, and hold on kindly.

cards.name: this chat

I answer from the site’s pages, the Library and my background notes (always labelled), I can walk you through any tool, work out a Battery Meter or CALC-01 score, and suggest a short path for what’s going on. what: The Objective Ledger is a free, plain-language program on understanding yourself and getting along with the people you share life with. It gives you a calm, shared way to see the work of running a life (including the invisible parts), fix the setup instead of blaming people, read your state before hard talks, and say things so they land.
It rests on the Five Pillars, and it works for yourself, partners, family, co-parents, friends, roommates, coworkers and caregivers. The ledger records the arrangement; it never puts anyone on trial.

cards.name: How it works
cards.what: How it works is a friendly tour of what the program looks at: your life situation (a new baby, a move or an illness can shrink what you can carry), your wiring (information, not a flaw), the patterns that show up when you write things down, and the static that lives between two people. It all rests on the Five Pillars.

cards.name: Is this right for you?

It fits when the same disagreements keep coming back, or when one person carries work the other can’t see, and you can also start on your own.

cards.name: Where your lens came from
cards.what: Where your lens came from is a guide to how growing up shapes the adult you. Each stage of development asks a big question (Is the world safe? Am I capable? Where do I belong? Can I be close without losing myself?), and the answers become understandings we carry forward and keep using. Something that happened while you were answering a particular question tends to go deeper. The guide also covers how family, culture, gender scripts, school and screens can hand us a mistaken view of ourselves, of other people, and of what we expect from them.
how: Read the simple version first: nine short ideas and a table of old understandings with fairer readings.
Write the rulebook from the home you grew up in: how love looked, what happened when someone was upset, how the jobs were split, when rest was okay, what asking for help meant.
For each rule, ask: do I still want this one?
When a reaction feels bigger than the moment, try the one-minute lens check: Where did I learn this? How old does this feel? Is it true here, with this person, now? What would the adult me choose?
With a partner or housemates, swap rulebooks on a calm day, then choose your own rules on purpose, like one owner per job.
cards.results: There’s no score. The point is to notice which understandings you chose and which were handed to you, so you can decide what to keep. It isn’t about blaming anyone: the adults who raised us were working with their own lenses too.
cards.ex: Maya felt “It’s always me” every time the kitchen was messy. Writing her rulebook, she saw the rule “whoever notices the mess cleans it” came from her childhood home. She and her partner gave the kitchen one owner each night, and the Sunday fights stopped.

cards.what: Roots & Wings is a gentle tap-through tool on the Where your lens came from page. You pick a trait or reaction you’d like to understand, like “I over-apologize”, “I can’t rest until everything’s done” or “I go quiet in conflict”, or just explore. Then it walks you through the stages of your life, from the early years up to now, with a few tap questions about the mood at home, the roles you took on, big changes and the unspoken rules. It’s self-reflection, not therapy or a diagnosis, and it never asks for details of anything painful.
how: Open Roots & Wings on the Where your lens came from page.
Pick one or more traits, write your own, or choose “I’m not sure yet, just explore.”
Tap through each life stage. Every question can be skipped, and there’s a “Something hard happened that I’d rather not name” option that asks nothing more.
An optional part asks, in general, how a hard time felt, what helped you get through, and how it may show up now. Never what happened.
Read your results, write one new rule you choose, and copy, print or save them. Nothing you type or choose is sent anywhere.
cards.results: For each trait you get gentle guesses from your own answers: where it may have started, what it protected back then, what it may cost now, how to notice it in the moment, and one or two small things to try this week, with words to say. They’re possibilities, not facts about you. Most families were doing their best with what they had; noticing where a rule came from isn’t blaming anyone. If a memory feels heavy, it’s okay to stop, and talking it through with a trained counselor can help.
cards.ex: Sam picked “I can’t rest until everything’s done.” Their answers showed being the responsible one in the school years, with “work comes first” as a home rule. The tool suggested one 15-minute rest before the list was done, and a new rule: “Rest is part of the work, not the prize for finishing it.”

what: Christian’s thirteen fields (neurobiology, psychology, philosophy, the art of debating, politics, behavioral science, economics, finance, business, holistic therapies, laughter therapy, music, aromatherapy) connect in every one of their 78 possible pairs. I sort them into three layers: 28 obvious, 29 hidden and 21 abstract. There’s also a chain where each field leads logically into the next, all the way round.

They connect along seven kinds of root: balance, signal and noise, feedback loops, limited capacity, ownership and structure, quiet incentives, and state and setting. Here are the 28 most obvious, where two fields share an idea in plain sight:
how: Psychology + Behavioral science (feedback loops): Habits beat willpower, especially when you’re tired. A routine too small to skip keeps going on the bad days. In the program: The 90-second check-in (WP-13).
Psychology + Neurobiology (state and setting): How you feel and how your nervous system is running are the same moment, seen from two sides. In the program: Today’s Weather.
Psychology + Holistic therapies (state and setting): Calm the body before the conversation. Words land better once the body has settled. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).
Philosophy + Business (ownership and structure): “Fair by promises” only works when the promises are written down: one owner per job. In the program: Chapter IV: two kinds of fair.
Behavioral science + Economics (quiet incentives): People follow what the setup quietly rewards, far more than what they intend. In the program: Pillar V.
Behavioral science + Business (feedback loops): Small, regular reviews catch problems while they’re small, in a company or a home. In the program: The monthly look-back (WP-04).
Neurobiology + Holistic therapies (limited capacity): A system past its limit can’t think its way back. Settle first, then talk. In the program: Breathe or the Night Garden.

Neurobiology + Aromatherapy (state and setting): What reaches the senses sets the body’s alert level. A noisy room makes every comment arrive louder. In the program: Chapter IV: giving a comment time to land.
Economics + Business (limited capacity): Time and attention get spent like any budget, and they run out like one too. In the program: The Lemonade Stand.
Economics + Finance (balance): Both keep accounts of a limited supply. Together they give the book its ledger and the idea of unbilled debt. In the program: The Preface: unbilled debt.
Finance + Business (ownership and structure): Internal controls give every job an owner and every entry a record. In the program: One owner per job (WP-03).
Holistic therapies + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Both start with the body and the senses, not the argument. In the program: Brain Breakers.

The art of debating + Psychology (signal and noise): Winning an argument and being understood are different goals. Debate trains the first; psychology reminds you the second is why you started talking. In the program: Say it so it lands (WP-09).

The art of debating + Philosophy (signal and noise): Debate grew out of philosophy: a claim is only tested when someone who disagrees gets to push on it. Telling what you know from what you assume is the first move of both. In the program: The Conversation Reader.

The art of debating + Politics (ownership and structure): Politics is debate with a decision attached: someone has to hear every side, then decide. A home needs a small version, with each voice heard first and one agreement at the end. In the program: Check-ins.
Politics + Philosophy (ownership and structure): Politics asks philosophy’s questions with real stakes: what is fair, who decides, and who is owed what. In the program: Chapter IV: two kinds of fair.

Politics + Behavioral science (quiet incentives): Good policy makes the right thing the easy thing: defaults, small rewards, less friction. Good house rules work the same way. In the program: Pillar V.

Politics + Economics (quiet incentives): Politics is largely a contest over who gets limited resources; economics counts them. In a home the resources are time, money and attention. In the program: The Lemonade Stand.

Politics + Business (ownership and structure): Governance means who is accountable for what, how decisions get made, and how to change them. “One owner per job” is governance for a household. In the program: One owner per job (WP-03).
Music + Psychology (state and setting): Music changes mood faster than words, and people use it on purpose: to pump up, to wind down, or to feel less alone. In the program: Drift: calm visualizer.
Music + Neurobiology (state and setting): Rhythm and sound reach the nervous system directly. Slow tempos tend to settle the body and fast ones lift it. In the program: Brain Breakers.

Music + Behavioral science (feedback loops): A song is a loop: a pattern that repeats with small changes. A habit tied to a tune or a time of day is easier to keep. In the program: The 90-second check-in (WP-13).

Music + Holistic therapies (state and setting): Music therapy is a recognized form of care: singing, drumming and listening help people settle, feel connected and find words. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).
Music + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Sound and scent both set the mood of a room before anyone speaks. A playlist in the kitchen does what a candle does. In the program: Brain Breakers.

Music + Laughter therapy (state and setting): Laughter is rhythm too: breath, bounce and sound, in time with other people. A shared laugh and a shared song both say “we’re in step.” In the program: Pause & Play.

Laughter therapy + Psychology (state and setting): A shared laugh tells the body “we’re safe.” Research on couples suggests that gentle humor during a disagreement can help calm it down. In the program: Turning Toward.

Laughter therapy + Neurobiology (state and setting): Laughing is linked with looser muscles and lower stress afterward. It’s a quick way to let the body know the alarm can stand down. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).

Laughter therapy + Holistic therapies (state and setting): Laughter yoga and therapeutic humor are part of the holistic toolkit: a whole-body reset that costs nothing. In the program: The Night Garden.

cards.name: the hidden connections
cards.pat: \b(hidden|less obvious|deeper|surprising|unexpected|subtle|secret|more) connections?\b|\bshow me (the )?hidden( ones)?\b
what: Here are the 29 hidden connections: fields that look far apart until you see the root they share.
how: Psychology + Philosophy (signal and noise): Intent isn’t impact, and most of what’s said in a conflict is a guess wearing the costume of a fact. In the program: The Signal Translator.
Psychology + Economics (limited capacity): We each remember our own effort best, so unseen work goes uncounted, though it spends real attention. In the program: Who did what (WP-01).

Psychology + Business (ownership and structure): Work with no clear owner lands on whoever notices first, and that person gets called controlling. Unclear ownership turns into hurt feelings. In the program: One owner per job (WP-03).
Psychology + Finance (balance): Goodwill works like a reserve. Thanks and repairs top it up; sharp words draw it down, and a low reserve makes small things feel big. In the program: Turning Toward.

Psychology + Aromatherapy (state and setting): The same sentence lands differently in a calm, quiet room. The setting changes what a person can take in. In the program: Chapter IV: where and when to talk.
Philosophy + Economics (balance): Efficient and fair aren’t the same thing. “It all got done” can hide who quietly did it. In the program: Chapter IV: two kinds of fair.

Philosophy + Finance (balance): Double-entry bookkeeping is a fairness idea: every entry has two sides, and a book that balances from one side only isn’t balanced. In the program: Your side, their side.

Behavioral science + Neurobiology (limited capacity): A tired body makes good habits harder. That’s why the program’s habits are tiny: they have to survive the worst day of the week. In the program: The 90-second check-in (WP-13).

Behavioral science + Finance (quiet incentives): A score you can raise by deleting the hard rows is rewarding the wrong thing. Keep the unowned jobs on the list. In the program: Chapter II: ownership clarity.
Behavioral science + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Cues in a room start habits. A cup of tea or a familiar scent can become your signal to slow down. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).
Neurobiology + Economics (limited capacity): Attention is scarce. Noticing, remembering and planning spend it, even when nobody sees. In the program: The mental load.
Neurobiology + Business (limited capacity): A team past capacity drops things, and so does a body. Both need a safety margin for the ordinary bad week. In the program: Chapter V: a capacity issue.
Neurobiology + Finance (balance): Your battery works like a balance sheet: leftover stress is a debt, and rest is the reserve. In the program: The Battery & Stress Meter (WP-02).
Business + Holistic therapies (feedback loops): Maintenance before breakdown. Care for people the way a good team cares for its systems, before the crisis. In the program: Check-ins.

The art of debating + Behavioral science (feedback loops): Arguments run on habit: the same lines, the same escalation. The best debate trick, restating their point before you answer, only works once it’s practiced enough to be automatic. In the program: The 90-second check-in (WP-13).

The art of debating + Economics (quiet incentives): In a debate the reward goes to whoever wins the room. At home the quiet reward for “winning” is the other person giving up, which costs far more than it saves. In the program: Chapter IV: two kinds of fair.

The art of debating + Finance (balance): A good argument keeps honest books: claims on one side, evidence on the other, and no entry without support. “You always…” is a debit with no receipt. In the program: The Conversation Reader.

The art of debating + Business (ownership and structure): Good meetings have a chair, an agenda and a decision at the end. A good hard talk at home needs the same: one topic, a turn each, and a named next step. In the program: Check-ins.

The art of debating + Neurobiology (state and setting): Reasoning well needs the thinking part of the brain, and it goes quiet on high alert. The best debate skill is knowing when your body can’t take part yet. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).

The art of debating + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Where an argument happens shapes how it goes. A crowded kitchen at dinnertime argues differently from a quiet walk. In the program: Check-ins: a good moment.

The art of debating + Music (signal and noise): Tone carries more than the words. The same sentence has a pace and a pitch, and spoken softly and slowly it lands differently than spoken fast and flat. In the program: The Signal Translator.

The art of debating + Laughter therapy (signal and noise): Humor in a disagreement can open a door or slam one. Laughing with someone shows you’re on the same side; laughing at them shuts the talk down. In the program: Say it so it lands (WP-09).

Politics + Psychology (signal and noise): Groups hear what they fear. How a message is framed changes how it’s received, and that’s as true at a dinner table as in a parliament. In the program: The Signal Translator.

Politics + Finance (balance): A budget is a political document: it shows what a group values. A week’s chores and hours are a household budget, and they show the same thing. In the program: Who did what (WP-01).

Music + Business (ownership and structure): An orchestra works because every player has a part and someone sets the tempo: one owner per job, and one shared beat. In the program: One owner per job (WP-03).
Laughter therapy + Behavioral science (feedback loops): A small, shared bit of silliness gets repeated and sticks. The in-joke is a habit that keeps closeness going. In the program: Turning Toward.
Laughter therapy + Economics (limited capacity): Joy refills what effort spends. A few minutes of play is a cheap way to top up the battery everything else draws on. In the program: Pause & Play.
Laughter therapy + Business (feedback loops): Teams that can laugh together tend to find it easier to say hard things early, while they’re still small. In the program: Check-ins.

what: Here are the 21 abstract connections: the deepest patterns, where the fields stop looking like separate subjects at all.
how: Philosophy + Behavioral science (feedback loops): Aristotle thought we become what we repeatedly do. Character, like a habit, is built by small acts, not by one big decision. In the program: Small and often.
Philosophy + Neurobiology (state and setting): If shutting down or getting revved up is a body doing its job, it isn’t a character flaw. That changes what blame means. In the program: Pillar II.

Philosophy + Holistic therapies (balance): A setup can be sustainable without being good for the people in it. Asking what makes the whole person well is a different question from “does it work?” In the program: Chapter II: what the number is not.

Philosophy + Aromatherapy (state and setting): What we take in through the senses shapes what we believe is true. Two people in one room may not be perceiving the same room. In the program: The Perspective Shifter.

Behavioral science + Holistic therapies (feedback loops): The smallest repeated acts, a breath, a daily check-in, a weekly look back, are rhythms, and rhythm is how a body and a relationship stay in tune. In the program: Chapter V: the rhythms.

Economics + Holistic therapies (balance): Rest isn’t time lost. It keeps the capacity that everything else spends, so skipping it is borrowing against next week. In the program: Wavelength: what fills you up.

Economics + Aromatherapy (quiet incentives): A room, like a market, carries costs nobody pays out loud. A rushed, noisy setting quietly taxes every conversation in it. In the program: Chapter IV: the setting.

Business + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Good workplaces are designed so the setting helps people do their best. A home can be too: a quiet corner for hard talks is a design choice. In the program: Check-ins: a good moment.

Finance + Holistic therapies (balance): A solvency read says whether an arrangement can last, never whether it’s worthwhile. Holistic care asks the other question: what makes the whole person well. In the program: Chapter II.

Finance + Aromatherapy (balance): Changing the setting costs almost nothing and pays back on every conversation held there: the cheapest investment in the whole program. In the program: Chapter IV: where and when to talk.

The art of debating + Holistic therapies (state and setting): Holistic care treats the whole person, and so does a good debate partner. The person across from you is tired, hungry or hurt as well as holding a position. In the program: The Perspective Shifter.

Politics + Neurobiology (state and setting): The nervous system treats a threat to “our side” as a threat to the self. Calm bodies compromise more, which is why settling comes before the vote. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).

Politics + Holistic therapies (balance): Public health and holistic care agree that wellbeing is shaped by the conditions around a person, not only by their choices. Fix the conditions. In the program: Pillar II.

Politics + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Politics knows the setting is a message: where the table is, how the room is laid out, who sits where. A home can use the same craft for hard talks. In the program: Check-ins: a good moment.
Politics + Music (feedback loops): Anthems and marching songs show how music binds a group. A shared beat is how a crowd starts to feel like one body. In the program: The theme song music video.

Politics + Laughter therapy (signal and noise): Groups have long used jokes and satire to say what can’t be said straight about power. At home, a light touch lets a sore topic be raised, if both people are in on the joke. In the program: Check-ins.
Music + Philosophy (balance): Thinkers since Pythagoras have asked why sound moves us. Harmony is a picture of fairness: different parts, each with room, in one piece. In the program: Echoes of Gold.
Music + Economics (limited capacity): Attention is what a song and a market both compete for, and it runs out. A noisy setting taxes every conversation held in it. In the program: Brain Breakers.

Then there are sixteen self-discovery chapters, a page on how the 9 inputs connect, an optional personal statement, and a way to compare codes with someone. It’s a fun way to describe preferences, not a diagnosis or a test that measures you. Nothing you type or choose is sent anywhere.
